{
  "Problem understanding": "You observe that two workers sometimes act as if they both hold the same distributed lock, leading to conflicting updates on an external resource, even though the underlying key-value store reports healthy status.",
  "Similar practical context": "This pattern matches the Jepsen study of etcd 3.4.3, where healthy key-value semantics coexisted with unsafe lock semantics that allowed multiple clients to hold the same lock and caused lost updates to an external critical section.",
  "Active hypotheses": [
    "The lock service is allowing duplicate holders because a lease has expired or a keepalive was delayed, so the lock ownership check is stale.",
    "The lock implementation does not re-validate lease validity before granting access, leading to stale lock holders after a lease change.",
    "The coordination primitive itself is unsound for protecting external state, regardless of lease timing."
  ],
  "First check": "Collect timestamps of lock acquisition, lease renewal, and conflicting updates, and look for a correlation where conflicts tend to occur shortly after a lease expiry or a missed keepalive.",
  "How to interpret the result": "If conflicts cluster around lease expirations or keepalive delays, this strengthens the lease-timing hypotheses and suggests the lock service is not guarding against stale ownership. If conflicts are uniformly distributed regardless of lease timing, it weakens those hypotheses and points more toward a fundamental unsoundness of the lock primitive for external resources."
}
